contents.name: Chapter 9 opening example: outcome misclassification dilutes an association
contents.reason: The example concerns measurement error in the outcome of a randomized causal study, while this pair's slope theorem concerns a latent covariate measured with error.

contents.name: 9.1 Measurement error
Technical Point 9.1 Independence and nondifferentiality of measurement errors
9.2 The structure of measurement error
Fine Point 9.1 The strength and direction of measurement bias
9.3 Mismeasured confounders and colliders
contents.reason: This section develops causal adjustment consequences of mismeasured confounders and colliders, which the assigned single-predictor error-model design does not claim.

contents.name: Fine Point 9.2 When mismeasured confounders are not a problem
contents.reason: The decision-information argument is about confounding adjustment, not the specified additive slope calculations or categorical measurement mechanism.

contents.name: 9.4 Causal diagrams without mismeasured variables
contents.reason: The causal-diagram simplification discussion supplies no result used by the pair's measurement definitions, regression slopes, or variance-split counterexample.

contents.name: 9.5 Many proposed causal diagrams include noncausal arrows
contents.reason: Its intervention and graph interpretation is a separate causal-DAG topic and is not part of the assigned measurement-error claims.

contents.name: Fine Point 9.3 Whether interventions are well-defined depends on the outcome
contents.reason: This addresses well-defined causal interventions rather than the statistical measurement mechanisms developed on this pair.

contents.name: Fine Point 9.4 Noncausal diagrams with well-defined statistical interpretations
contents.reason: The discussion is about statistical interpretations of causal graphs, outside the pair's univariate error-model proof obligations.

contents.name: 9.6 Does it matter that many proposed diagrams include noncausal arrows
contents.reason: The section continues causal-graph identification arguments that the assigned page neither states nor uses.

contents.name: Fine Point 9.5 Connection to the front door formula
contents.reason: The front-door identification discussion is a separate causal-identification result and does not support these measurement-error claims.

contents.reason: Adjustment changes the regression target and requires a separate proof; the assigned attenuation claim is restricted to one predictor.

contents.name: 3.1.3 Regression with multiple error-prone covariates
contents.reason: The multiple-covariate formulas have additional covariance terms and are not claimed by this pair's simple one-predictor theorem.

contents.name: 3.1.4 Common non-linear regression models
contents.reason: Nonlinear regression has different bias behavior and is explicitly outside the pair's linear slope results.

3.2.1 Single covariate regression

contents.reason: Adjusted regression coefficients require the covariate-specific attenuation analysis not included in the assigned one-predictor page.

contents.name: 3.2.3 Regression with multiple misclassified covariates
contents.reason: Multiple misclassified predictors do not have the simple attenuation form and are outside the planned pair scope.

contents.name: 3.2.4 Other common situations

contents.reason: Outcome-error formulas differ from covariate-error formulas and are not stated on the assigned page.

contents.name: 3.4 Effects of measurement error on estimating the distribution of a variable
contents.reason: Distributional estimation is a separate target from the assigned regression-slope and identifiability claims.

contents.name: 4.3.2 Physical activity
